Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Mumbai, India at 2026-02-12 12:30 IST (UTC+0530) (2026-02-12T07:00:00Z in UTC), at latitude 19.076 degrees and longitude 72.8777 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 56.797 degrees and its azimuth is 169.915 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 16.173 degrees and its azimuth is 230.855 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 25.16 percent illuminated, 60.074 degrees from the Sun, and 401170.4 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To give you an honest estimate: **No, you will not be able to see it.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the specific data you provided:

### 1. The "Washout" Factor (The Biggest Obstacle)
The most significant factor is the **Sun's altitude (56.797°)**. At nearly 57 degrees, the Sun is high in the sky, creating intense atmospheric scattering. This creates a "washout" effect where the blue of the sky is at its peak intensity. 

Because the Moon is only **25% illuminated** (a waxing crescent), it is a very thin sliver of light. A thin sliver of reflected sunlight cannot compete with the sheer volume of scattered sunlight in a bright daytime sky. It would be like trying to see a dim flashlight beam while standing directly under a stadium floodlight.

### 2. The Angular Separation
The Moon is **60.074 degrees** away from the Sun. While this is a decent distance, it isn't enough to move the Moon out of the "glare zone." In astronomy, the "glare" of the Sun extends significantly beyond its immediate position. At 60 degrees, the Moon is still deep within the brightest part of the daytime sky.

### 3. The Moon's Altitude
At **16.173 degrees**, the Moon is relatively low on the horizon (South-West). While this means it isn't "hidden" behind the zenith, it also means it is looking through a thicker layer of the atmosphere (more air mass) than if it were higher up. This further dims the already faint crescent.

### 4. Human Perception
As an ordinary adult with normal eyesight, your pupils will be constricted to tiny points because of the bright daylight. This reduces your ability to pick up low-contrast objects. To see a 25% crescent in broad daylight, you would typically need a telescope or, at the very least, high-powered binoculars to "isolate" the Moon from the surrounding blue.

### The Verdict
If you look toward the South-West (Azimuth 230°), you will see a very bright, washed-out sky. You might see a slight "smudge" or a faint grayish area if you squint intensely, but **you will not see a distinct lunar crescent.** 

**Honest Estimate:** 0% chance of seeing it with the naked eye.
